'''Bryaceæ''' (brī-ā′sẹ̄-ē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Bryum'' + ''-aceæ''.] An order of mosses, comprising all the true mosses, as distinguished from the peat-moss (''Sphagnum'') and the schizocarpous mosses (''Andreæa''). See ''moss''.

'''Bryanite''' (brī′an-īt), ''n.'' [From their founder, William ''Bryan'' (about 1815).] One of a Methodist body, more properly known as ''Bible Christians'' (which see, under ''Bible'').

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|brutality|701|Bryum}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''brutality''' (brö-tal′i-ti), ''n.''; pl. ''brutalities'' (-tiz).   [= F. ''brutalité'', < ML. ''brutalita(t-)s'', < ''brutalis'': see ''brutal''.]   '''1.''' The quality of being brutal; inhumanity; savageness; gross cruelty; insensibility to pity or shame.
{{smaller block|It is to be noted that the unredeemed ''brutality'' implied by the stories of the earlier gods is in the stories of the later considerably mitigated.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Sociol., § 107.}}}}
'''2.''' A savage, shameless, or inhuman act.
{{smaller block|The mere ''brutalities'' exercised in war by enraged conquerors are perhaps to be laid out of view in estimating the practical effects of despotism. {{right|''Brougham.''}}}}
='''Syn. 1.''' Barbarity, ferocity, truculence.

'''brutalization''' (brö″tal-i-zā′shon), ''n.''   [< ''brutalize'': see ''-ation''.]   The act of brutalizing, or the state of being brutalized. Also spelled ''brutalisation.''
{{smaller block|Scruples of conscience respecting the rectitude of their cause would paralyze officers and soldiers. So that a certain ''brutalization'' has to be maintained during our passing phase of civilization.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Study of Sociol., p. 190.}}}}

'''brutalize''' (brö′tal-īz), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''brutalized'', ppr. ''brutalizing''.   [= F. ''brutaliser'', < ''brutal'': see ''brutal''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To make brutal, coarse, gross, or inhuman; lower to the level of a brute.
{{smaller block|<poem>Strange! that a creature rational, and cast
In human mould, should ''brutalize'' by choice
His nature. {{right|''Cowper'', Task, i.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|Degraded and ''brutalized'' by a long course of oppressive misgovernment. {{right|''Whately.''}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become brutal, inhuman, or coarse and beastly. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|He . . . ''brutalized'' with them in their habits and manners.{{right|''Addison'', Freeholder.}}}}

Also spelled ''brutalise.''

'''brutally''' (brö′tạl-i), ''adv.'' In a brutal manner; cruelly; inhumanly; in a coarse, gross, or unfeeling manner.
{{smaller block|''Brutally'' repulsed by the attending lictors.{{right|''Goldsmith'', Alcander and Septimius.}}}}

'''brute''' (bröt), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [= F. ''brut'', fem. ''brute'', = Sp. Pg. It. ''bruto'', < L. ''brutus'', heavy, unwieldy, stupid, insensible, unreasonable; particularly applied in later L. to the lower animals.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Senseless; unconscious.
{{smaller block|Not walking statues of clay, not the sons of ''brute'' earth.{{right|''Bentley.''}}}}
'''2.''' Wanting reason; animal; not human: as, a ''brute'' beast.
{{smaller block|<poem>A creature . . . not prone
And ''brute'' as other creatures, but endued
With sanctity of reason. ''Milton'', P. L., vii. 507.</poem>
I was amazed to see such actions and behaviour in ''brute'' beasts.{{right|''Swift'', Gulliver’s Travels, iv. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' Characteristic of animals; of brutal character or quality.
{{smaller block|''Brute'' violence and proud tyrannic power.{{right|''Milton'', P. R., i. 219.}}}}
{{smaller block|The oppressed invoked the power of Christianity to resist the tyranny of ''brute'' force.{{right|''Bancroft'', Hist. U. S., II. 454.}}}}
'''4.''' Blunt or dull of sentiment; without sensibility; rough; uncivilized; insensible.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''brute'' philosopher who ne’er has proved
The joy of loving or of being loved. ''Pope.''</poem>}}
'''5.''' Not associated with intelligence or intellectual effort; unintelligent; irrational.
{{smaller block|A more legitimate kind of valour that, showing itself against the untamed forests and dark ''brute'' Powers of nature, to conquer nature for us.
{{right|''Carlyle.''}}}}
'''6.''' Harsh; crude. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The ''brute'' fact is expressed in the phrase “One man’s meat is another man’s poison.”
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', A Mortal Antipathy, vii.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Brute, Brutish, Brutal, Beastly, Bestial.'' ''Brute'' is the most general of these words, and remains nearest to the distinguishing difference between man and beast, irrationality: as, ''brute'' force. ''Brutish'' is especially uncultured, stupid, groveling: as, brutes and still more ''brutish'' men. ''Brutal'' implies cruelty or lack of feeling: as, ''brutal'' language or conduct. ''Beastly'' expresses that which is altogether unworthy of a man, especially that which is filthy and disgusting in conduct or manner of life. ''Bestial'' is applied chiefly to that which is carnal, sensual, lascivious: as, ''bestial'' vices or appetites.}}
{{smaller block|The feats of Hercules . . . were triumphs of ''brute'' force.
{{right|''Sumner'', Fame and Glory.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''brutish'', the animal instincts, as is often the case, had been developed earlier than the intellectual qualities.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, xxi.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To mask . . .
With a glassy smile his ''brutal'' scorn.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, vi.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>This filthy simile, this ''beastly'' line.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Ep. to Sat., ii. 181.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And since his ways are sweet,
And theirs are ''bestial'', hold him less than man.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Coming of Arthur.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A beast, especially one of the higher quadrupeds; any animal as distinguished from man. {{smaller block|''Brutes'' may be considered as either aërial, terrestrial, aquatic, or amphibious.
{{right|''Locke.''}}}}

'''2.''' A brutal person; a savage in disposition or manners; a low-bred, unfeeling person.
{{smaller block|An ill-natured ''brute'' of a husband.
{{right|''Franklin.''}}}}

'''brutehood''' (bröt′hu̇d), ''n.''   [< ''brute'' + ''-hood.'']   The state of being a brute; the condition of being brute or brutish in nature or habits.
{{smaller block|It is modestly suggested, by no means dogmatically affirmed, . . . that the influences that have raised mankind from ''brutehood'' to its present condition have not yet expended their force.
{{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXVI. 461.}}}}

'''brutel†''', ''a.'' A Middle English form of ''brittle.''

'''brutely''' (bröt′li), ''adv.'' '''1.''' In a rude manner; as a brute.   ''Milton.''—'''2.''' By brute force; without intelligent effort; blindly. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Property will ''brutely'' draw
Still to the proprietor.</poem>
{{right|''Emerson'', The Celestial Love.}}}}

'''bruteness''' (bröt′nes), ''n.''   [< ''brute'', ''a.'', + ''-ness.'']   The state of being brutal or a brute. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>That sire he fowl bespake: Thou dotard vile,
That with thy ''brutenesse'' shendst thy comely age.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. viii. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|The immobility or ''bruteness'' of Nature is the absence of spirit.
{{right|''Emerson'', Nature.}}}}

'''brutification''' (brö″ti-fi-kā′shọn), ''n.''   [< ''brutify'': see ''-fy'' and ''-ation.'']   The act of brutifying; the act or state of becoming or making brutal or degraded.
{{smaller block|She would have saved thee, as I said before, from ''brutification.''
{{right|''J. Baillie.''}}}}
{{smaller block|This ultra-Circean transformation of spirit and ''brutification'' of speech we do not find in the lighter interludes of great and perfect tragedy. {{right|''Swinburne'', Shakespeare, p. 194.}}}}

'''brutify''' (brö′ti-fī), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''brutified'', ppr. ''brutifying''.   [< F. ''brutifier'', < L. as if *''brutificare'', < ''brutus'', brute, a., + ''-ficare'', < ''facere'', make.]   To bring into the condition of a brute; degrade the moral or physical state of; make senseless, stupid, or unfeeling.
{{smaller block|Not quite ''brutified'' and void of sense.
{{right|''Barrow'', Works, III. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|It has possessed only two secrets for governing, . . . to drain and to ''brutify'' its subjects. {{right|''Bentham.''}}}}

'''brutil†''', ''a.'' A Middle English form of ''brittle''.

'''brutish''' (brö′tish), ''a.''   [< ''brute'', ''n.'', + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Of or pertaining to a brute or brutes.
{{smaller block|<poem>There his welwoven toyles, and subtil traines,
He laid the ''brutish'' nation to enwrap.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Astrophel.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Wandering gods disguised in ''brutish'' forms.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 481.}}}}
'''2.''' Like a brute; characteristic of brutes. (''a'') {{smaller|Unfeeling; savage; ferocious; brutal.}}
{{smaller block|Bombarding of Cadiz; a cruel and ''brutish'' way of making war, first begun by the French.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, August 25, 1695.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Not riches
Can purchase him, nor honours, peaceably,
And force were ''brutish''.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''?), Nice Valour, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Gross; carnal; bestial.}}
{{smaller block|It is the ''brutish'' love of this world that is blind.
{{right|''Baxter'', Saint’s Rest, xiv.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') Uncultured; unrefined; ignorant; stupid; insensible.}}
{{smaller block|Brutes and ''brutish'' men are commonly more able to bear pain than others. {{right|''N. Grew'', Cosmologia Sacra.}}}}
{{smaller block|They were not so ''brutish'' that they could be ignorant to call upon the name of God. {{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Pol., v. § 35.}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Brutal, Beastly'', etc. (see ''brute''), dull, barbarous, animal, sensual.}}

'''brutishly''' (brö′tish-li), ''adv.'' In a brutish manner; grossly; irrationally; stupidly; savagely.   ''South.''

'''brutishness''' (brö′tish-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being brutish in nature, disposition, or appearance; savageness.

{{smaller block|Not true valour, but ''brutishness.'' {{right|''Bp. Sprat.''}}}}
{{smaller block|In many of the Cynocephali, longitudinal osseous ridges are developed upon the maxillæ, and greatly increase the ''brutishness'' of their aspect. {{right|''Huxley'', Anat. Vert., p. 398.}}}}

'''brutism''' (brö′tizm), ''n.''   [< ''brute'' + ''-ism.'']   Brutal instincts or tendencies; bruteness; animality.

'''brutting†''' (brut′ing), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''brut'', ''v.'']   Browsing.

{{smaller block|Hornbeam preserves itself best from the ''brutting'' of the deer. {{right|''Evelyn'', Sylva, I. vi. 2.}}}}

'''brutum fulmen''' (brö′tum ful′men).   [L.: ''brutum'', neut. of ''brutus'', insensible; ''fulmen'', a thunderbolt: see ''brute'' and ''fulminate.'']   A harmless thunderbolt; mere noise like thunder; empty noise and nothing more.

{{smaller block|The actors do not value themselves upon the clap, but regard it as a mere ''brutum fulmen'', or empty noise, when it has not the sound of the oaken plant in it. {{right|''Addison'', The Trunkmaker at the Play.}}}}
